newsitem.title: FRANCE: French election - key campaign comments on EMU.
newsitem.headline: French election - key campaign comments on EMU.

text.p: European monetary union has become a key theme behind the campaign in France's parliamentary election, in which the combined left led the ruling centre-right RPR-UDF coalition in the first round of voting. The second and final round is due on Sunday. Following is a selection of comments by leading politicians.
PRESIDENT JACQUES CHIRAC
-- Do you really want to put the socialist ideas of yesteryear back in the saddle?
I hope the majority which you will choose does not take the risk of weakening European integration. (May 27)
-- Let us not forget that (France) will only be able to defend its interests if it is capable of speaking with a single voice, a strong voice. (May 20)
SOCIALIST LEADER LIONEL JOSPIN

-- We are for the single currency, and have been from the beginning. One can be against the single currency, and that's a respectable stance, but it would not be the position of a government. (May 29)
-- We want to respect the spirit and the letter of the (Maastricht), treaty, a treaty which allows for an interpretation of the convergence criteria in terms of trend.

We are setting four conditions on the launch of a single currency...a European economic government next to the European Central Bank, membership of Italy and Spain, a solidarity and growth pact, a competitive euro...
They are not 'take it or leave it' conditions, but the opposite -- they are the basis for a realistic discussion among the countries creating the euro (May 21)

-- The stability pact adds conditions which do not feature in the Maastricht treaty. The pact is a 'super-Maastricht' of sorts and a concession which the French government made absurdly to the Germans or certain German circles.
Therefore, I have no reason to feel committed to it.

I want a French government which will be less timid and less passive on the European level. We've got a government which shows a lack of punch in Europe by taking a docile line on the demands of others. (May 20)
(on any power-sharing with the Communist party)
-- There won't be both a 'yes' and a 'no' to the single currency. There will be a single line, the one which (we) propose to the French people.

Then it will be up to the Communists to make up their minds freely if we have a majority. They will only be able to participate in government if they are ready to commit themselves to that line. (May 7)

-- If to respect the criteria of three percent, which Germany will probably not respect, if to do that we have to impose, with the jobless rate we have...a new austerity cure on the country my answer is no. No to the absolute respect of the three percent criterion.
We will have one year to relaunch a real dialogue with Germany. We won't say yes unconditionally to monetary union if that leads to a worsening of unemployment (April 20)
PRIME MINISTER ALAIN JUPPE.
(on EMU entry criteria)
-- Everybody knows that when the European Council meets in March or April of 1998, when we examine the situation, entry into the single currency will be a political decision.
Therefore it is evident that the second decimal place...will be interpreted with intelligence and not with an accountant's rigour. (May 27)
-- We cannot leave it up to the European central bank to do everything. There should be an economic government for Europe, as we have been asking for months and have now begun to obtain
(on power-sharing between right-wing president and opposition Socialist party)

-- It would be a shambles in Europe, firstly because the Socialists and Communists don't agree among themselves...and also because the Socialists' economic policy, with extra spending and deficits, would push us off track for European (monetary) union." (May 20)
PHILIPPE SEGUIN, NATIONAL ASSEMBLY SPEAKER (RPR).
-- We are in a straitjacket. I dare hope that once the euro is launched and we no longer need to convince German public opinion, we will loosen it.
There should not be a petty bookkeeper's approach to the entry conditions for the euro. The maximum number of countries must participate.
A target of three percent of deficits in a period of expansion is not virtuous. In a period of austerity it is masochism.
(on whether Paris should honour the Maastricht treaty)
France's signature is committed....That signature must be honoured (May 27)
FORMER FRENCH BUDGET MINISTER NICOLAS SARKOZY (RPR).

-- I would prefer we respect the criteria if possible, (but) there is a general consensus in the (ruling centre-right) majority...we will not refuse monetary union because we are not exactly at 3.0 percent.
(on the need to avoid competitive devaluations)
It would be better to have the southern countries (Italy, Spain and Portugal) in the euro rather than exclude them. (May 29)
COMMUNIST PARTY LEADER ROBERT HUE
-- If Jacques Chirac speeded up the election timetable, it is because, to meet the criteria for joining the single currency, he wants to impose further austerity on our people as soon as possible.
It can be seen today that the conditions for joining a single currency, as they are defined by the Maastricht treaty, are unacceptable to the people.
We remain partisans for the organisation of a referendum allowing our people to decide on joining the single currency in a sovereign way. (May 6)
FAR-RIGHT NATIONAL FRONT LEADER JEAN-MARIE LE PEN
-- This sort of Europe, dominated by Germany and organised in 'Laender'-like provinces ignoring existing nations, will make Hitler's dream come true. (May 15)
